title: How to Keep a Consistent Writing Style in Claude Projects
content:
Screenshot of support.anthropic.com (source)

One way to get more consistent writing out of Claude is to stop re-explaining your voice in every chat and move those rules into a Project. Project instructions tell Claude the specific context and requirements for a particular project, and they only apply to chats inside that project - so every new conversation in that workspace starts with your style rules already loaded. Pair that with uploaded samples of your own writing and, optionally, account-level instructions or a skill, and you can get more consistent output over time (results vary).

Here's the setup, start to finish.

What You'll Need

Screenshot of anthropic.com (source)

  • A Claude account. Anthropic's help center says Projects are available to all users, including free accounts, with a maximum of five projects on Free (source), and the pricing page lists Projects as "Up to 5" on Free. Paid plans add more usage and features.
  • 3–5 pieces of writing you're genuinely happy with (published posts, newsletters, client emails) saved as text or PDF.
  • A browser, or the Claude desktop/mobile app. Web is easiest for file uploads.
  • Allow time to prepare the rules and review test drafts. A 20-minute setup is only a rough estimate; calibration may take longer.

Step 1: Create a Project for one type of writing

Screenshot of claude.com (source)

Open Claude, go to Projects in the left sidebar, and create a new project. Name it for the output, not the topic - "Weekly Newsletter," "Client Case Studies," "LinkedIn Posts."

This matters more than it sounds. A single catch-all "Writing" project forces you to write vague instructions that fit everything, which is exactly how you end up with generic output. One project per format lets you get specific about length, structure, and tone.

Step 2: Write project instructions that actually constrain Claude

Inside the project, find the instructions field (Claude labels this area for project instructions or custom instructions, depending on your version) and add your rules there. Anthropic recommends using project instructions to provide project-specific context, set guidelines for a workflow, establish requirements for a set of tasks, and define roles or perspectives Claude should adopt - and notes they're especially useful when you need Claude to maintain consistent context across multiple conversations in the same project.

The trick is writing rules Claude can actually check itself against. "Be conversational" does nothing. These do:

  • Sentence and paragraph limits. "Paragraphs max three sentences. Vary sentence length - don't write three long ones in a row."
  • Banned words and tics. List the words you never use. Mine would include "delve," "leverage," "unlock," "in today's fast-paced world." Be specific; a concrete blocklist gives you something specific to check in the resulting draft.
  • Structural rules. "Open with the answer, not context. No summary paragraph at the end. Subheads are sentence case."
  • Point of view and address. "First person singular. Address the reader as 'you.' Never 'we' unless describing the company."
  • Formatting. "Bullets only for lists of three or more parallel items. No bold inside body paragraphs."
  • A voice anchor. One or two sentences: "Sounds like a senior colleague explaining something over coffee - confident, specific, occasionally funny, never salesy."

Keep instructions concise and focused on general context, key guidelines and the role Claude should take. This follows Anthropic's usage and length guidance, not a measured comparison of one page versus three pages.

Step 3: Upload real samples as project knowledge

Instructions describe your voice; samples demonstrate it. Add 3–5 finished pieces to the project's knowledge files.

Two rules for picking them. First, upload only work that's already in the voice you want - one off-brand piece drags the average. Second, upload finished, published versions, not drafts. If you have an internal style guide or a list of approved product terms, add that too.

Then add one line to your instructions telling Claude what to do with the files: "Before drafting, review the sample posts in project knowledge and match their rhythm, paragraph length, and level of directness."

Step 4 (optional): Use account-level instructions or a skill for your voice

Anthropic's help center says Styles are moving to skills: custom styles are migrated to skills, the styles menu is being removed, and the Concise, Explanatory and Formal default styles will no longer be available after the migration (source). Migrated styles are disabled by default; you enable them under Customize > Skills and can activate one in a chat with a slash command in the form /{style-name}-style. If you'd rather not use skills, the same article says you can describe the tone, format and approach in Instructions for Claude, which apply to all your conversations.

For a writing voice, that gives you two optional layers on top of the Project: account-wide instructions (applied to every chat, so keep them general) or a skill you enable when you need it. Because this area is changing, check the current help center articles on personalization and creating custom skills before relying on a specific menu.

Step 5: Calibrate with a test piece, then lock it in

Run one real assignment. Compare the draft to your best sample side by side and note every place you'd edit. Then, instead of fixing the draft, fix the instructions: turn each edit into a rule and paste it into the project.

Try a few calibration drafts and review the results yourself; no fixed number of rounds guarantees consistency. If you repeatedly make the same correction, consider adding a specific rule to the instructions.

FAQ

Do I need a paid plan for this? No. Anthropic's help center says Projects are available to all users, including free accounts, with up to five projects on Free. Paid plans add more usage and features.

What's the difference between profile preferences, project instructions, and styles?

Anthropic's guidance: use Instructions for Claude for account-wide settings affecting all your conversations, project instructions for guidance specific to one project, and skills to customize how Claude formats and delivers responses. (Its personalization article still carries a "paid plans only" note next to project instructions, but its projects article says free accounts can create up to five projects.)

The three can be used independently or together.

Will my style rules leak into my other chats? No. Project instructions only apply to chats within that project. Instructions for Claude apply to all your conversations, and an enabled skill is available in your account, so keep them general or switch them off when you're doing unrelated work.

How many samples should I upload? Three to five relevant pieces is a suggested starting point, not a tested optimum. Use writing you own or have permission to share. Do not upload confidential client emails without authorisation.

Wrap-Up

Consistency in Claude comes from stacking three things: a dedicated Project, instructions written as checkable rules, and real samples Claude can pattern-match against. Set it up once for each format you write regularly, then treat your instructions as a living document - every repeated edit is a rule you haven't written down yet.

Correction note (October 2026): This post was revised because Claude's current help center says Projects are available to free accounts (up to five), not only paid plans, and because Styles are being migrated to skills, so the earlier custom Style step and preset descriptions were out of date. Sources: Projects help article, Claude pricing, Styles are moving to skills, Personalization features.

This is a documentation-based suggested workflow. No controlled hands-on style benchmark was run.
